author: Lucy Mangan
description:
Film-maker Poppy Jay meets a woman who uses her kids for money-making content and another who treats her husband like Jesus. You just wish for even more interrogation – and for a therapist to step in

Like film-maker and journalist Poppy Jay’s previous (excellent) documentary, Young, British and Anti-Abortion, her latest offering should come with a warning and blood pressure medication for all women watching. Some men, too, I’m sure, but you’ll forgive me if I can’t quantify the proportion.

In Young, British and Tradwife, Jay interviews three women in the UK who are advocating the lifestyle that first took off as a social media phenomenon in the US (where the evangelical Christianity and social conservatism with which it is enmeshed are stronger influences than here). Each of the trio has been chosen with c
title: Young, British and Tradwife review – TV this frustrating should come with a blood pressure warning

author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer in Cincinnati and Jeff Rueter
description:
As he prepares to depart for Manchester United, the outgoing US coach held court on a number of topics, including what he’d change about soccer in America

Outgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.

So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.
title: Pochettino: I’d tell Guardiola to ‘take it’ if he’s offered US coaching job

author: Richard Partington, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu
description:
Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up

Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits.

In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

Continue reading...
title: Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

author: Auzzy Byrdsell
description:
Johnson was working on the USS St Louis and was inside a steam drum when the attacks took place

The oldest known survivor of the Pearl Harbor attack died Saturday aged 106 years old. Freeman Johnson, a fireman below the deck during the attack, died in his home in Massachusetts, according to the Boston Globe.

Only 11 known Pearl Harbor survivors are still living, all of whom are centenarians.

Continue reading...
title: Freeman Johnson, oldest survivor of Pearl Harbor attack, dies aged 106

author: Lucy Mangan
description:
After the week we’ve had, you may not feel ready to watch this brilliantly powerful film about the toxic manosphere and its impact on relationships. But do make the time

I would understand, after the week in the news we’ve had, if you were not feeling quite ready to deal with the new instalment of I Am … , Dominic Savage’s anthology series that examines different aspects of women’s lives and tends to do so with merciless precision and in pitiless detail.

The stories are worked out with the female actor central to each: Vicky McClure in 2019’s inaugural I Am Nicola, about coercive control, Samantha Morton in one about the vulnerabilities poverty brings, Suranne Jones imploding under the accumulated pressures of midlife and trying to be everything to everyone because nobody else will pick up the slack, and other heavy hitters like Lesley Manville and Kate Winslet starring with younger actors to showcase different generational concerns. The latest was devised with Nicola C
title: I Am Helen review – Nicola Coughlan is absolutely superb in this terrifying must-watch

author: Ewan Murray at Berit Sitterstadion
description:
A match that should have been about 103 was instead about four. Andy Robertson is due huge acclaim for becoming the most capped player in Scotland’s history but how the full-back will wish the moment arrived in different circumstances. A second string Switzerland team pulled Scotland apart, raising further and significant questions about the suitability of Sébastien Pocognoli to carry out the job his paymasters boldly entrusted him with. Scottish FA giddiness about Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke, a hugely successful leader of the national team, is looking increasingly ridiculous.

This was a horrible night for Pocognoli, who is under serious pressure just three months into his tenure. Scotland’s players looked a rudderless, disillusioned lot. Pocognoli has never previously managed in international football, which renders it reasonable to ask his
title: Switzerland roll over sorry Scotland to increase the pressure on Pocognoli

author: Associated Press
description:
The US president oscillates between strike threats on Iran and insisting the war ‘militarily is effectively over’

A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than 8-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.

Continue reading...
title: Third US aircraft carrier brings thousands more troops to Middle East

author: Barney Ronay
description:
Another 3-2 win in Spain brings the lure of a golden new hyper-future – but it did not pan out that way last time

I may have the body of a weak and feeble German, but I have the heart and stomach of a manager of England. And I think it foul scorn that Spain should dare to invade the borders of my realm. Or, for that matter, any one of 24 qualified teams for Euro 2028, because at the end of the day there are no easy games at this level, I’ve always said that.

The words, there, of Thomas Tuchel, England’s Faerie King, speaking to TalkSport shortly after the glorious 3-2 defeat of the Spanish possession armada at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Continue reading...
title: Tuchel and England must learn lessons of history, Seville and Southgateism | Barney Ronay

author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
description:
DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.

Continue reading...
title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
description:
Andy Wigmore says he wants his Enough Official group to join forces with Michael Gove-backed Stay Out movement

The Brexit wars were a bitter period in political history, fraught with tension and badmouthing – and that was just between the different leave campaigns.

Now as a new incarnation of Dominic Cummings’ Vote Leave looks set to re-enter the political fray, so too does a rival anti-EU campaign from the team behind Leave.EU, who ran their own unofficial campaign backed by Nigel Farage.

Continue reading...
title: People behind Leave.EU and Vote Leave launch new incarnations of pro-Brexit campaigns

author: Pippa Crerar Political editor
description:
Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis

In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.

The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.

Continue reading...
title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment

author: Ben Jennings
description: Continue reading...
title: Ben Jennings on the jobs crisis for young people – cartoon

author: Will Unwin
description:
⚽️ Nations League updates from the 7.45pm GMT kick-offs
⚽️ Live scoreboard | Follow us on Bluesky | And mail Will

Jurgen Klopp v Xavi Hernandez is the sort of matchup we all want on our football calendar. Germany v Netherlands is a cracker of a fixture at any time but with the respective head coaches getting their feet under the table, we are starting to get a greater understanding of how their teams will play.

Scotland are in Switzerland looking to build on beating North Macedonia on Friday night. Super John McGinn scored twice on that occasion and the Tartan Army know he will be significant again if they are to pull off a result against the Swiss.

Conti
title: Switzerland v Scotland, Germany v Netherlands, and more: Nations League – live

author: Emine Sinmaz
description:
Comments come after Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Russell Brand, had said she wanted a change in law

A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggered age of consent.

Walliams, 55, has been accused by multiple women of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found.

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers
title: Woman accusing David Walliams of grooming her backs staggered age of consent call

author: Nils Pratley
description:
The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration

Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes.

This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words.
title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley

author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Emma Graham-Harrison ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
description:
Deadly floods in Gaza have created a dire humanitarian crisis, as the governments of Australia, Canada, the UK and Italy call on Israel to allow the safe passage of critical aid to civilians before winter sets in. Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents, with sanitation infrastructure also destroyed by storms. Supplies including food, medicine and water and 150,000 tents are being held by Israel at the border, while the UN warns of the spread of diseases. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent, Emma Graham-Harrison

Continue reading...
title: ‘Let the aid in’: Deadly winter approaches in Gaza - The Latest

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Volunteers despair as the charity sets about closing local branches and restructuring

Samaritans old and new will, I’m sure, have been just as shocked as I was by your article (‘Is anyone up for a fight?’: The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November). Many, though, will not be surprised. I was a volunteer for 26 years in three branches. The work was demanding and life-changing; the experience is so transformative that it gives every part of society people who are strong enough to bear others’ burdens and able to share their pain. We don’t stop being listeners when we stop being volunteers.

During my time, I found that the people at the top were detached from what went on at branch level. It is not news to me that they cannot understand how central to the work each local branch is and how important every human contact is to those who need to talk.
title: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Savitri Hensman says financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest

Alan Milburn has a track record of so-called cost-cutting measures that waste billions of pounds in public money while making health worse. The private finance initiative was an expensive mess, though it did help huge companies and rich people get richer. It is less surprising that he wants more benefits for young sick and disabled people slashed than that the government might go along with this (Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund, 12 November).

Financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest. The high number of young people not in education, em
title: Why Alan Milburn’s Pip plan is a mistake | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Joanna Elson of the Independent Age charity is concerned about poverty among pensioners and says ministers need to think hard before making changes

You report (11 November) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock.

It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggl
title: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Thomas Altebaeumer notes that under the proposed scheme, UK students in Europe would pay domestic fees, as EU students studying in the UK would

Vicky Wolmuth is angered that the UK government is able to find £450m to subsidise UK universities for admitting EU students while UK students are struggling with student debt (Letters, 10 November).

She appears to have missed that, under the proposed scheme, UK students in Europe would pay domestic fees, just as EU students studying in the UK would. Fees in the UK are among the highest in Europe. This is a political choice.

Continue reading...
title: A fair deal on fees for EU and UK students | Letters

author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
description:
Forces across England and Wales struggle amid financial pressures described as worst for decades

Police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government.

Paul Sanford, the chief constable of Norfolk police and the finance lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), said exceptional financial support was needed if forces across England and Wales were to remain operationally viable.

Continue reading...
title: Police ‘retreating from streets’ due to major funding crisis, chief constables say

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
• Gloucester flyer excelled during thrashing of Japan

  • Joseph in pole position for place on the wing

Will Joseph is poised to be rewarded for his five-try heroics with another England start against the All Blacks on Saturday as Steve Borthwick’s team seek back-to-back victories against New Zealand for the first time since 2003.

Joseph starred on the right wing against Japan, scoring five tries to equal the men’s national record in his first England start last Saturday. The Gloucester flyer has been in scintillating form all season and, after Immanuel Feyi-Waboso was struck down with injury against Australia, Borthwick wasted little time in turning to Joseph. In what would represent another bold call by the head coach, it is understood Joseph is in pole position for a wing berth again as England
title: Will Joseph poised to start for England against All Blacks after five-try burst

author: Sid Lowe in Madrid
description:
While the head coach, players and Spanish press were magnanimous in defeat, there was pride mixed in with disappointment – and confidence the future is still bright

“With every game, defeat gets closer,” Luis de la Fuente had said and on Sunday night it finally came. Spain had lost only one competitive game since Scotland in March 2023 back when the coach hadn’t won anything and didn’t look like he ever would – and that solitary loss was on penalties in the 2025 Nations League final. Statistically, they said, penalties don’t count, so while Portugal lifted the trophy that night, the team that won the European Championship and World Cup in the summers either side also claimed a Fifa record of 44 official g
title: Spain in pain as historic run ends but De la Fuente feels best is yet to come

author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
description:
Renowned centre of Shakespeare studies, which is part of University of Birmingham, to move to its Edgbaston campus

“Near-philistine”, “ignorant”, “unbelievably stupid”, “terrible”, “extraordinarily sad and shortsighted”, “an appalling act of cultural vandalism”, “a disaster” and “an absolute disgrace”.

Such has been the furious reaction to news that the Shakespeare Institute, a much-loved and internationally renowned centre of scholarship, is to leave its home in Stratford-upon-Avon, the playwright’s place of birth, and move to Birmingham.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Near-philistine’: fury greets Shakespeare Institute plan to leave Stratford-upon-Avon

author: Polly Toynbee
description:
The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country

This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. An end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old.

There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service, careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his
title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee

author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey , produced by Nada Smiljanic and Annie La Vespa , music by Axel Kacoutié ; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
description:
It is a big week for Andy Burnham as two of his big policy priorities enter the spotlight. On Tuesday, the Milburn review of welfare for under-25s is published, which could ignite old Labour tensions over benefit cuts.

Then, later this week Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit to discuss a potential new deal. But, as Pippa has signalled, cabinet ministers have told Burnham to put the brake on some of the discussions to ensure the government is not out of step with the public.

Is it too little too late?

Continue reading...
title: Andy Burnham told to put a brake on moves for a new EU deal | Politics Weekly

author: Michael Savage Media editor
description:
Presenter says she will remain at the corporation working on show launching in 2027, as search for successor begins

The BBC has confirmed Emma Barnett is stepping down as a presenter of Radio 4’s Today programme, setting off the broadcaster’s latest search for a new name to co-host its flagship news programme.

The official announcement came after months of speculation about Barnett’s future on the show. Her last appearance will be broadcast on Wednesday.

Continue reading...
title: Emma Barnett steps down from BBC Radio 4’s Today programme

author: John Crace
description:
The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe

So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser.

For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never
title: Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech | John Crace

author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
description:
Treasury-backed review says customers of banks such as Monzo and Revolut often rely on physical cash services

Digital banks like Monzo and Revolut could be forced to pay towards high street banking facilities, after a government-backed review outlined plans to protect face-to-face financial services across the UK.

The access to banking review, which was released on Monday, was commissioned by the Treasury earlier this year, and addresses the dwindling options for nearly 3 million people who regularly rely on in-person banking across the UK.

Continue reading...
title: Digital-only banks could be forced to fund high street banking

author: Associated Press
description:
Clancy’s first trial on charges of first-degree murder ended in mistrial after jurors couldn’t reach unanimous verdict

A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.

Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.

Continue reading...
title: Judge sets Lindsay Clancy retrial for March in killings of her three children

author: Ed Aarons
description:
• Frank’s first job since Spurs dismissal in February

  • He has been promised funds for January signings

Thomas Frank has been confirmed as Crystal Palace’s manager after Pierre Sage was sacked last week. Frank, out of work since being dismissed by Tottenham in February, was quickly identified as Palace’s main target and has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal at the Premier League’s bottom club.

Frank spoke to Palace in the summer about succeeding Oliver Glasner but decided he was not ready to return to the dugout because he wanted to take a break from football.

Continue reading...
title: Thomas Frank confirmed as Crystal Palace manager after Pierre Sage’s sacking

author: Emma Dibdin
description:
About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them

Naming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions.

That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years.

Continue reading...
title: Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help

author: Bryan Armen Graham
description:
• USA face Canada for women’s ice hockey world title

  • Puck drop at 1pm US eastern time (6pm GMT/7pm CET)

  • Rivals have combined to win all 24 previous editions

  • Reach out to Bryan on Bluesky or by email

Bryan will be here shortly to marshal our coverage of the women’s ice hockey world championship final between the United States and Canada. In the meantime, here’s the Associated Press report on Sunday’s semi-final twin bill:

The United States and Canada will renew their rivalry in the final of the women’s ice hockey world championship on Monday.

In the semi-finals on Sunday, defending champions the US blanked Finland 5-0 before Canada shut out Sweden 3-0.

Continue reading.
title: United States v Canada: women’s ice hockey world championship 2026 final – live

author: Fiona Harvey, Graham Readfearn, Damien Gayle and Gabrielle Canon in Antalya
description:
Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.
title: Cop31 draft text is attempt to ‘draw out parties’ to find agreement, president of talks says

author: Dan Milmo and Lauren Almeida
description:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’

Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, as he joined Silicon Valley heavyweights in demanding the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.

The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

Continue reading...
title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO

author: Simon Burnton
description:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Glory. Imminent and near-enough-guaranteed glory. That, surely, is what we’re looking at from the giddy heights England reached in crushing Spain 3-2 on Sunday. “If we can find that first hour consistently, we are a genuine favourites for the next tournament,” roared Steven Gerrard, a statement he believed in so much he then said it again using different words: “The first 60 minutes told me, from watching it, that we’re capable of winning the next tournament. That’s the big thing to take away.” Thomas Tuchel reckoned England had reached the “highest level football-wise in all aspects of the game”. This is the kind
title: Football Daily | England’s Nations League triumph in Spain sparks familiar rush to glory

author: Ariana Baio
description:
Letter to Warren, likely to chair Senate banking committee, echoes warnings to Democrats moving to investigate Trump

The Trump administration has warned Elizabeth Warren, the senior Democratic senator expected to chair the powerful Senate banking committee, she could face potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into Donald Trump.

US attorney Aaron Reitz of the southern district of Texas sent Warren a warning letter, stating that she appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates”.

Continue reading...
title: DoJ warns Elizabeth Warren of ‘consequences’ unless she preserves Trump records

author: Stuart Heritage
description:
This Netflix documentary offers a fascinating look at how Brand’s behaviour wasn’t simply tolerated; it was actively celebrated

Last week was quite the week. Coming within a few days of each other, the sentencing of Russell Brand and the allegations about David Walliams have felt dizzying. As well as all the elation that justice has been served in relation to Brand, and the admiration for the women who saw that it was, there’s also an underlying sense of exhaustion about the sheer grubbiness of it all.

With this in mind, the thought of
title: Russell Brand: Open Secret review – ​a real tribute to the journalists and victims who brought him to justice

author: Guardian Staff
description:
They only make this noise when humans are around – and, as you may have noticed, it is one of the bossiest sounds in the animal kingdom …

Name: Miaow.

Age: Evolved over millennia.

Continue reading...
title: Miaow! What your cat is really trying to tell you

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Pattinson is a character actor whose talent for inscrutable appraisal may mean a new era for 007. Will this more willowy, classy Bond leave sexism in the shadows?

• New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
• Share your thoughts on the casting

If it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality.

And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily
title: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw

author: Lewis Gordon
description:
Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact

• The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
• Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus
• Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA

A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio
title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world

author: Lucy Pavia
description:
We spent months putting hundreds of presents to the test – here is how we whittled them down

• The best Christmas gifts for 2026

If you struggle with the idea of Christmas creep – when the festive season appears to start earlier every year – spare a thought for the team here at Filter HQ. We’ve been in Christmas mode since we packed away last year’s decorations, testing hundreds of presents for our magnum opus: the big 2026 Christmas gift guide.

All 369 (we did say it was big) gifts on this year’s list were put through their paces by a crack team of testers covering all ages and tastes. Fashion writer and stylist Sam Deaman – who tested men’s accessories and nightwear – says his partner got fed up with him parading “yet another” pair of py
title: From pyjama parades to blind biscuit taste tests: how we made our ultimate festive gift guide

author: Simon Tisdall
description:
The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice

It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet his final downfall remains far from certain.

As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary l
title: Though Trump is giving him the cold shoulder, Netanyahu is pulling out all the stops to cling to power. And he just might | Simon Tisdall

author: Aaron Bower
description:
No free-to-air coverage and uncompetitive teams meant England fans all but missed a tournament that caught fire in the southern hemisphere

So, that was the Rugby League World Cup. It may have gripped you from start to finish or it may have passed you by without recognising it was even happening. It probably depends on where you are in the world: the tournament showcased many things, but, perhaps most of all, the widening gulf between the two hemispheres.

There have been some magnificent and overwhelming positives. The primary one appears to be that those in charge in Australia – soon to be in charge in England, but more on that shortly – have realised there is value in international rugby league. For too long the NRL has disregarded the international game, but it has come alive again in recent years.
title: Rugby League World Cup was a triumph in Australia and invisible in the UK | Aaron Bower

author: Nick Ames
description:
• Body of 138 members complains to European Commission

  • Uefa and the European Football Clubs power targeted

The Union of European Clubs has submitted a formal complaint against the stranglehold Uefa and European Football Clubs maintain on football within the continent, dramatically escalating its efforts to obtain recognition by governing bodies and dilute the power held by the elite.

The complaint, filed to the European Commission on Monday, challenges the memorandum of understanding (MoU) between EFC and Uefa. That agreement, which runs until July 2033, stipulates that EFC is the “sole body” representing European clubs. The UEC, which was founded three years ago and has 138 members from 25 national associations, aims to afford a voice to those beyond the established powers and has long sought to be allowed a formal presence in the
title: Union of European Clubs escalates fight for football influence with formal complaint

author: Ruth McHugh-Dillon
description:
The brand had cherrypicked fragments of the Futurist Manifesto for decoration – as if they referred to a hydrating night mask, rather than a violent new world order

  • Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

In a group interview for a luxury skincare brand – the one everyone jokes is a cult – a tall woman in a sack dress told us they preferred to hire people without any previous experience in skincare. “We find they need to unlearn a lot of what they think they know.”

I was 19, happy to kneel on the converted warehouse’s concrete floor to demonstrate my enthusiasm for teamwork, building a structure from drinking straws with other retail candidates. And when I got it, that job was my gateway to Melbourne. I’d just moved and suddenly my life was brimming with cool and cleve
title: A job that changed me: Washing hands at a luxury skincare brand, I learned how fascism could feel ‘aesthetic’

author: Ranjana Srivastava
description:
Every year I receive a letter from the daughter of a patient I treated. It’s an act of unbelievable grace in a job that often feels thankless

Many years ago, in early November, I received a note.

It read: “Dear Doctor, Dad would have been 78 years old today. Of course, no amount of time would have been enough. We think of him and miss him every day.”

Continue reading...
title: As an oncologist, I’ve received my fair share of thank you notes, but nothing like this | Ranjana Srivastava

author: Helena Horton
description:
Popular edible golden oyster classed as high-risk invasive species because of negative impact on woodlands

They have been viewed for years as the ideal Christmas gift for the culinary-minded, but experts have now warned that grow-your-own mushroom kits should be blacklisted from a spot under the tree.

An international group of mycologists, including experts from the Royal Horticultural Society, have said many of these kits, which allow people to easily grow mushrooms at home as a delicious addition to stir-fries and other dishes, contain invasive species.

Continue reading...
title: Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk

author: Matt Hughes
description:
• Ineos wanted £10m for alleged refusal to return yacht

  • Out-of-court settlement ends plan for a 2028 trial

Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group has reached an out-of-court settlement with Sir Ben Ainslie over the £180m yacht their companies built for the 2024 America’s Cup. Ratcliffe and Ainslie worked closely together during two cycles of the America’s Cup culminating in Ineos Britannia becoming the first British crew to win the challenger series two years ago, but fell out over plans for a third bid, with Ineos announcing last year that it had “reluctantly withdrawn its challenge” for next year’s event in Naples.

Ineos launched a legal action in March after expressing “surprise” that Ainslie’s Athena Racing had opted to keep using Britannia, which was beaten 7-2 by Emirates Team New Zealand in 2024, in the
title: Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group settles with Ben Ainslie over America’s Cup dispute

author: Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen and agencies
description:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda items, but many hope world’s three biggest nuclear powers will talk about denuclearisation

The unprecedented meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, cements Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.

Continue reading...
title: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China

author: Selected by Natasha Rees-Bloor
description:
The Guardian’s picture editors select photographs from around the world

Continue reading...
title: Snow machines, a shepherd and a plastics protest: photos of the day – Monday

author: Helena Horton
description:
Move reflects growing demand for outdoor swimming as Britain heats up and follows campaign by MPs

Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in outdoor swimming.

Outdoor pools were built across the UK in the 1930s. The often beautiful, art deco constructions were made as a cheap way to provide access to healthy activity during the summer.

Continue reading...
title: Under-threat lidos get lifeline as Andy Burnham sets up fund to rebuild pools

author: Jess Elliott Dennison
description:
Easy cheesy dumplings with the perfect level of lightness and squidge

Making gnocchi from scratch can be a bit of a faff midweek. However, these ricotta-and-parmesan-based dumplings are so easy to throw together, and always come out light and with just the right amount of squidge. Sage and brown butter feels the right sauce at this time of year, but you could serve them with a simple tomato sauce instead. Any leftover dumplings work a treat thrown into a brothy, minestrone-type soup.

Continue reading...
title: Jess Elliott Dennison’s quick and easy recipe for ricotta dumplings with sage butter, rocket and lemon | Quick and easy

author: Beril Eski in Mexico City
description:
The female-led unit in Mexico City has cut gender-based murders from a historic high in 2021. Now, there are hopes to appoint specialist teams and prosecutors nationwide

Paz Rodríguez woke up about 5am at her home in Milpa Alta, a suburb of Mexico City, on 20 March 2021. She thought about her plans for the day: pick up yellow lilies and cacti from her mother’s house and sell them in the market. Later that evening, they would cook mole, a traditional Mexican dish, together.

She reached for her phone, which was flooded with texts from her sister, Oliviera Rodríguez. “Mum’s dog is barking a lot,” she had written. “I keep calling and she won’t respond.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘These men feel protected’: how Mexico’s first femicide squad is turning the tide on record killings

author: Robert Reich
description:
The party’s big-tent approach has caused post-election feuding in the past. But a pair of singular goals can prevent it

Democrats usually suffer big tent disease. To win, they put together such large coalitions of voters – working class, middle class, Black people, Latinos, women, young people, moderates, liberals – that once they’re in office, intraparty feuds often threaten their agenda.

Will it happen again when they take power in January? I don’t think so. Two outside forces will keep Democrats glued together.

Continue reading...
title: Two reasons Democrats can overcome infighting next year | Robert Reich

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
A sense of menace permeates a verdant private golf course in water-deprived Manila, peopled with submissive tee-girls and geisha-style caddies catering to the male clientele

A spectacle filled with dreamlike tableaux, off-centre framing and slow trance-like zooms, Filipiñana is an elegant and politically pointed feature debut from the Filipino director and London Film School graduate Rafael Manuel, developed from his award-winning short film of the same name. It is a melancholy satire on caste shame, sexual politics and land exploitation in the Philippines, symbolised by a private golf course in Manila, an artificial landscape as depthless and surreal as the gardens in Last Year in Marienbad. Irrigating the vivid greens and undulating fairways requires oceans of precious water – water that, in the course of one unbearable heatwave, is rationed for the sweating lower orders in the city, wa
title: Filipiñana review – melancholy satire on sexual politics and land exploitation in the Philippines

author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
description:
Exclusive: Study shows people taking action against far-right intimidation such as 75-year-old taking to his bike at 2am to remove flags

Flag campaigns and far-right intimidation have sparked a wave of grassroots anti-racism organising across England in the past 12 months, according to new research.

The Institute of Race Relations (IRR) warns that the widespread displays of St George’s cross and union jack flags have been accompanied by racist abuse and violence, with flags deliberately placed outside schools, mosques and care homes.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Visceral response’: flag campaigns inspire anti-racism organising across England

author: Emanuele Giulianelli at the Bruno Benelli Stadium
description:
Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side

It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by Italian Serie C side Ravenna, to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence.

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was, not only in the squad but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion to Serie B.

Continue reading...
title: A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
description:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine

Ukraine has hit the Kerch Bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.

A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.

Continue reading...
title: Ukraine hits Kerch Bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea

author: Guardian community team
description:
We would like to hear your thoughts on the reopening of the Brexit debate

Andy Burnham has announced that he will sign a new deal with the EU, arguing the UK has “lost more than we gained” since Brexit.

“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say at the lord mayor’s banquet in London on Monday, ahead of a summit with European leaders to secure agreements he says could raise GDP by £17bn.

Continue reading...
title: Share your thoughts on Andy Burnham’s plan for a new EU deal

author: Suzanne Wrack, Tom Garry, Sophie Downey, Mitul Samji and Réshma Rao
description:
Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the informatio
title: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

author: Tom Ambrose
description:
Letter to likely chair of Senate Banking Committee is latest warning to Democrats about their potential plans following midterms success

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances.

Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.
title: DOJ warns Elizabeth Warren over Trump investigations – US politics live

author: Barry Glendenning
description:
Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League clash with Kosovo

The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure. Tuesday night’s final Nations League group match at home to Kosovo presents a chance for progress or yet another opportunity to showcase a frustrating habit of messing things up. For 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years. Set up in a compact, attack-minded formation they carried credible threat against hosts managed by Ralf Rangnick, but to nobody’s great surprise, the home substitute Sasa Kalajdzic broke the deadlock, scrambling home the winner from a needlessly conceded and poorly defended corner.

This late lapse neatly captures the contradiction bedevilling this Ireland team under Hallgrímsson. Over the past 12 m
title: Republic of Ireland have plenty of promise but are unable to shake the self-sabotage

author: Exclusive by Nick Ames
description:
• Diallo may have candidacy confirmed by Uefa on Tuesday

  • Uefa executive committee meeting to discuss matter

The French Football Federation president, Philippe Diallo, is a surprise late contender to run for the Fifa presidency and could have his candidacy confirmed by Tuesday.

The search for a Uefa-backed candidate to run against Gianni Infantino has been taken to the wire, with Wednesday the deadline for those planning to contest the Fifa election in March. Diallo has emerged as the favourite to be put forward after plans to enlist a decorated former player or manager did not reach fruition, although other names are understood to remain under consideration. Uefa’s executive committee will discuss the matter on Monday and the approval of its 55 member associations would be sought.

Continue reading...
title: French football head Philippe Diallo is shock contender to fight Infantino for Fifa job

author: Raphael Rashid
description:
Broadcaster TV3 appears to cut footage of Thai drag performers and gay Philippine jury spokesperson

Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened.

Continue reading...
title: Eurovision organisers criticise Malaysian removal of LGBT+ footage in first Asian contest

author: Temi Wilkey
description:
Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance

Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost. The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died.

Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community ali
title: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey

author: Ali Martin in Hobart
description:
• Leg-spinner made one appearance in recent tri-series

  • Liam Dawson has retained place in Australia

Adil Rashid has become a slightly peripheral figure in England’s white-ball plans this winter, with his close friend Moeen Ali openly criticising the management and warning it could damage their World Cup chances next year. After a hand injury at the end of the home summer, Rashid made one low-key outing during the recent tri-series in Pakistan. While he began the Australia tour with figures of four for 35 in the warm-up match in Perth, Liam Dawson has remained the chosen spinner for the first two one-day internationals.

Harry Brook, the captain, claimed the initial preference for Dawson in Perth was down to the conditions encountered and a more all-round game that lengthens the batting. His continuation on a flatter surface in Adelaide raised more eyebrows, even if the move to leave out Jamie Overton did risk a longer tail without him.

<
title: Moeen Ali warns England ‘cannot win the World Cup’ by sidelining Adil Rashid

author: Guardian community team
description:
We are looking for people to share their stories of misdiagnosis, how they realised this had happened, and perhaps found another diagnosis

Last month the actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. She announced that she had the condition in 2021, and has spoken candidly about her experiences of it, becoming a prominent advocate for people living with MS.

“I’m back at square one ... I don’t know what’s going on with me.” Applegate said on her podcast MeSsy, adding: “There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS.”

Continue reading...
title: Tell us: have you been misdiagnosed with a medical condition?

author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
description:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

Continue reading...
title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests

author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
description:
Move follows Russell Brand trial, in which his barrister argued comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not ‘resisted’

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial.

Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers amid concern over the tactics deployed by the comedian’s counsel. In his letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Norris said it was “unacceptable” for the profession to “perpetuate myths” about rape victims in court, and warned that those who broke the rules could face disciplinary action.
title: Barristers could be barred from practice over use of rape myths, warns justice secretary

author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
description:
As he releases new solo album Human Grace, and lives with Parkinson’s disease, the synthpop heartthrob will take on your questions

His group A-ha were one of the defining acts of 80s synthpop, thanks to hits such as Take On Me and Hunting High and Low – and lead singer Morten Harket is now about to release one of the most poignant albums of his career. As he does so, he’ll be joining us to answer your questions.

Born and raised in Norway where he still lives, Harket struck out for London in 1982 with his bandmates Paul Waaktaar-Savoy and Magne Furuholmen, determined to make it in the music business. They had a killer opening gambit with Take On Me – which climaxed with Harket’s startlingly pristine falsetto singing. After a couple of failed releases, it finally hit the big time in 1985, topping charts all over the world including in the US: the first Norwegian band to do so there.
title: Post your questions for A-ha frontman Morten Harket

author: Kenneth Zindondo
description:
Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles

The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika.

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.

Continue
title: ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters

author: Duncan Riddell
description:
The latest in our series of writers picking their most comforting rewatches is a tribute to Curtis Hanson’s insightful 2000 comedy drama

I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all.

I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Even the misadventures of the film’s professor, Grady Tripp (M
title: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie

author: Phil Hoad
description:
Peter Stylianou’s watchably unsettling tale of unbalanced minds and Unidentified Aerial Phenomena does its best to please

Drone shots are two-a-penny in cinema these days, but it’s a mark of this £80,000 British indie sci-fi’s visual astuteness that it largely avoids them in a film plagued by drone-like entities. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank.

Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Already not at ease among his mates, Kate gets a ribbing when she repeats her UFO story (or Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, as they are called these days). And there are knowing glances about her psychiatric history: she once fended off an abusive boyfriend at knifepoin
title: The Nice Ones review – invasion of the sunny personality snatchers

author: Rian Evans
description:
Theatr Brycheiniog, Brecon
Puccini’s short comic opera comes to life with Richard Studer’s touring production, which leans into its commedia dell-arte elements

In Dante’s Inferno, Gianni Schicchi de’ Cavalcanti, a 13th-century Florentine knight, was consigned to the eighth circle of hell for having been an arch-impostor. Puccini’s Gianni Schicchi, however, gets away with his blatant fraud, impersonating the newly deceased Buoso Donati and cheating his greedy relatives out of a large part of their rich uncle’s inheritance – albeit that they plotted with him to overturn the original will – to bag the best for himself.

In this last of the Il Trittico triptych, Puccini allowed himself a lot of fun, and that too was the main ingredient in Mid Wales Opera’s SmallStages touring production. Tightly choreographed, with comedic energy and over-the-top characterisations, the commedia dell’arte element here bordered on farce, not least as the lugubrious crocodil
title: Gianni Schicchi review – fraud, fun and farce with the gutsy Mid Wales Opera

author: Andrew Sparrow
description:
Ed Balls, shadow chancellor at the time, said he had warned Labour leader not to go ahead with ‘ridiculous’ interview

Good morning. There are two issues that will dominate the political news this week – the EU reset, and the Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment – and this morning there are new lines on both of these issues.

Andy Burnham has set out “three tests” for the deal that he is due to agree with the EU at a summit on Friday. Tonight he is giving the traditional prime ministerial speech to the lord mayor’s banquet in London, which by convention focuses on foreign policy, and, according to the overnight briefing from Downing Street, he will announce three tests. No 10 says:

Ahead of this week’s UK-EU Summit, the prime minister will set out three tests for any agreement:

-First, it must be consistent with the manifesto and the Government’s red lines.

It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes – where no one is prepa
title: Ed Miliband defends doing 2015 election interview with Russell Brand, saying he was ‘taking him on’ not endorsing him – UK politics live

author: Alex Kirshner
description:
The San Francisco 49ers quarterback was long seen as the beneficiary of the tools at his disposal. This season, he’s setting fire to that narrative

The Cowboys entered this week having given up the second-most points in the NFC, but there was a particular elegance to the beating Brock Purdy put on them as the 49ers moved to 8-1 with a 46-40 shootout win in front of a sullen Jerry Jones in north Texas. Purdy has presided over lots of routs since he took over the offense in 2022, but this particular defeat of the Cowboys had a unique feel to it.

Purdy, who is often dismissed as benefiting from a hospitable 49ers system, was a wrecking crew. That was true in the statistical sense, as Purdy closed with 389 yards and three touchdowns on 22-of-28 passing. Later in the game, it became true in the literal sense as Purdy ended one of his greatest games in style.

Continue reading...
title: Brock Purdy was once dismissed as a system guy. Now he is THE guy

author: Natasha Walter
description:
I’ve seen how a new wave of hatred has changed the way the sector goes about its work, and now a report details this crisis. It must be a wake-up call

  • Natasha Walter is the founder of Women for Refugee Women

There is a small charity that brings its local community together every day in a centre made bright with flowers grown in its own little garden. People, old and young, migrant and citizen, eat meals together made from food that would otherwise go to waste. The children play with donated toys, the grownups learn English together. Last summer, they had an outing to the seaside and posted some of the joyful pictures online.

They won’t do that again.

Natasha Walter is an author and honorary professor at Queen Mary University of London. She is the founder of Women for Refugee Women

Continue reading...
title: Migrants targeted, charity workers menaced for helping them. Are we that kind of society? | Natasha Walter

author: Robert Kitson
description:
The plot twist in Cardiff that nobody saw coming suggests the northern hemisphere is remobilising in time for next year’s World Cup

What does it take to beat the All Blacks in Cardiff? “I’ll never forget the pressure they put us under. I don’t think we were a better team than New Zealand, but there was a certain spirit in the Welsh side which pulled us through.” The vivid recollections of the late, great Cliff Morgan on Wales’s famous victory in 1953 could just as easily have applied to the long-awaited modern-day sequel on Saturday.

Seventy-three years. The last time it came to pass was the year Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay officially became the first people to conquer Everest. Some bookmakers had even stopped taking bets on an All Blacks win; in
title: Wales’ epic upset against All Blacks offers fresh hope for rank outsiders | Robert Kitson

author: Nick Ames and Matt Hughes
description:
Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome

It will be one of the most eagerly anticipated documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into exactly how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino. Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of d
title: European football body’s secret plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

author: Clive Paget
description:
Lapwood/Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir
(Sony)
Lapwood’s arrangements of Howard Shore’s film score are in gothic overdrive played on Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral organ, while her Elvish additions and an ethereal choir shine

When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive.

But wait, there’s more. Reckoning the symphony would benefit from the human voice, she incorporated a handful of songs, performing them live – in Tolkien’s Elvish dialect – while playing the Nidaros Cathedral organ in Trondheim, Norway. The results are frequently convincing, though the folksy music of the Shire is less ef
title: Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost album review – Anna Lapwood

author: Stacey Soluade
description:
People come together online to support one another with small voluntary donations to ease financial worries

For some time people struggling with debt have used social media to document what they owe, swap advice and hold themselves accountable as they try to pay it off. Some have built large audiences around their repayment journeys, using views and engagement to generate income through creator payment schemes, livestream gifts and donations from followers towards their debts.

Now the idea is being taken a step further: rather than one person building an audience to help clear their own debt, strangers are creating communities to help pay off one another’s.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Strangers gave me £2,409’: the online community helping people in debt

author: Fiona Sturges
description:
She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit

Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.

That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a
title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

author: Charlie Moloney
description:
Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.

It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

Continue reading...
title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU

author: Donna Ferguson
description:
Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.

Continue reading...
title: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction

author: Anna Tims
description:
DWP admits it is making a mistake that affects his immigration status but says it can’t put it right

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is knowingly paying me too much local housing allowance because of a system glitch and it could have serious implications for my partner’s immigration status.

I am entitled to shared accommodation allowance as I am under 35 and claim universal credit. However, the DWP is paying me the higher one-bedroom rate for couples.

Continue reading...
title: Housing allowance glitch threatens my partner’s leave to remain

author: Dougie Wallace
description:
Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became the title

Growing up in Scotland, our family was one of many who kept their photographs in an old shortbread tin. The lid usually showed a castle beside a loch, a stag, a Highland coo and plenty of tartan. It was always sunny.

Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid is Scots for “my little tin of shortbread”. The title started as a warning to myself: don’t make the Highlands look like a tin of shortbread.

Yellow backpacks and trekking poles rest on benches, with Ben Nevis rising behind

Continue reading...
title: Ma Wee Tin O’Shortbreid: a journey in search of the real Highlands

author: Ben Aitken
description:
The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’?

I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign.

I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do
title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’

author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
description:
Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design

Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)

Processor: Apple M6

RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB

Storage: 1, 2 or 4TB SSD

Operating system: macOS 26.
title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation

author: Hollie Richardson, Rachel Aroesti and Alexi Duggins
description:
The Guardian’s new twice-weekly show unpicks all the biggest cultural moments. Plus, what is it like to grow up as a YouTube kidfluencer?

Is SNL UK funnier than the original? Does it matter if a pop star can sing? The Guardian’s Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko host this twice-weekly culture videocast. On Thursdays, they zoom in on a big cultural moment with fresh takes. On Sundays, they have a culture swap: introducing each other to a TV series, book, film, album, play or podcast with which they’re obsessed. Hollie Richardson
Widely available, episodes twice-weekly from Thursday 19 November

Continue reading...
title: Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko are your new culture guides: best podcasts of the week

author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
description:
Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say

UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter.

Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say.

Continue reading...
title: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches

author: Phuong Le
description:
Angela Schanelec’s famously uncompromising work takes on a new warmth in this sometimes playful study of everyday emotional turmoil

The elliptical cinema of German film-maker Angela Schanelec is often described as uncompromising. This latest work, however, radiates a striking warmth. We see a marriage tearing at the seams, but this untethering is devoid of the usual dramatic flourishes. On an ordinary day like any another, construction worker Thomas (Vladimir Vulevic) notices a missed call from his wife, Carla (Agathe Bonitzer); when he phones back, she doesn’t pick up. The event holds little significance for the mild-mannered man; he carries on his usual chitchat with his co-workers, mundane catchups that unfold over static, tableaux-like shots.

This deceptive calm is ruptured, however, when Thomas finds Carla sobbing helplessly on a park bench. A se
title: Accidents, emotional affairs and impromptu Leonard Cohen dancing - My Wife Cries review

author: Melissa Denes
description:
From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy

In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalizatio
title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures

author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
description:
Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis

Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found.

While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.

Continue reading...
title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’

author: Hollie Richardson and Phil Harrison
description:
The two stars are brilliant in Dominic Savage’s I Am Helen. Plus: Wayne Rooney and a bunch of celebrities land in the jungle. Here’s what to watch this evening.

9pm, Channel 4
Helen and Steve have been together for five years. They’re generally happy, but something is starting to feel wrong. Steve wants to get married and have children; Helen is still undecided. But that’s not all. Steve is bored by the sex they have, too. And he’d rather Helen didn’t pursue her career dreams. There’s also a workmate who is whispering ideas into his ear. As Helen and Steve’s relationship unravels, so, too, does a compelling exploration of toxic masculinity and its poisoning of relationships. This two-parter is the latest brilliant drama in Dominic Savage’s Bafta-winning I Am anthology, with leads Nicola Coughlan and Joe Cole putting in career-best performances. Hollie Richardson
title: TV tonight: Nicola Coughlan and Joe Cole’s powerful drama about a toxic relationship

author: Australian Associated Press
description:
• Khawaja says he made promise to Warner six years ago

  • ‘There is always a cost in everything you do,’ he says

Usman Khawaja has insisted he tried to balance standing up for David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft with the cost to other players with his bombshell ball-tampering claims.

In a newly-released podcast on Monday, Khawaja defended his claims that the entire team were aware of ball tampering in 2018, and said any lost relationship with Cricket Australia would be a small price to pay.

Continue reading...
title: ‘A small price to pay’: Usman Khawaja defends book claims amid deepening rifts

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
The president reiterated criticisms he made last week – saying Ukraine’s use of Elon Musk’s satellite-based service continued to face restrictions. What we know on day 1,727
